claims.text: At 1400–1600°C, equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
At 1400–1600°C, equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Thermally stable, low-energy grain-boundary complexions form in WTaTiVZr at the specified high temperatures.
Nanoscale Zr-rich precipitates develop in situ in WTaTiVZr during high-temperature loading.
Nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates may develop in situ in WTaTiVZr during high-temperature loading.
The proposed grain-boundary states and nanoprecipitates pin dislocations.
The proposed grain-boundary states and nanoprecipitates facilitate grain-boundary sliding.
Dislocation pinning and facilitated grain-boundary sliding delay crack initiation in WTaTiVZr.
Delayed crack initiation shifts WTaTiVZr from brittle failure toward more ductile failure.
Multicomponent alloying induces grain-boundary states in WTaTiVZr that are distinct from those in pure tungsten.
Multicomponent alloying facilitates in situ nanoprecipitate formation at mechanically important sites.
Pure tungsten forms fewer or no comparable nanoprecipitates under the same test conditions.
Pure tungsten exhibits less grain-boundary sliding than WTaTiVZr under identical high-temperature loading.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit a mixed or transgranular ductile fracture mode under the proposed conditions.
Pure tungsten will exhibit predominantly intergranular brittle fracture under the proposed conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from approximately 1400°C to 1600°C in inert atmospheres.
Initial grain-size or dislocation-structure differences could dominate the measured mechanical response and limit the proposed mechanism's validity.
Processing-induced defects or phase segregation may contribute to the plastic-strain and toughness differences.
